transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

I came in because my mind just doesn’t seem to hold onto things anymore. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I used to do without even thinking—and the numbers and words just scatter on me. It’s been really upsetting.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with your memory and concentration?
About three weeks now. It started after my older sister died, and since then I just haven’t been able to keep my thoughts together the same way.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the time since your sister passed away?
Yes. Most days I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Even when my wife is being kind to me, I still feel like I’m way down at the bottom of a well, like I can’t really reach anything.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy, like hobbies or spending time with family?

Yes. I just don’t feel like doing the things I used to. I haven’t touched the wood pieces sitting on my bench, and I’ve skipped choir planning and chess. Even fishing sounds like more effort than it’s worth now, and that really isn’t like me.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or lacking energy most days?
I’m not really sure. I mean, I haven’t been paying close attention to that. I don’t feel like myself, but I can’t say for sure if it’s tiredness exactly.
Have you been feeling like you’re not worth much or that you’re failing others, even when you’re not?
I don’t know. I haven’t really thought about it that way. I feel bad a lot, but I’m not sure I’d say I’m thinking I’m worthless or failing people.
Have you found it hard to focus on things, like reading or following a conversation, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

Yes. That’s actually part of why I came in. My mind just won’t hold onto things anymore. I’ll sit down to write a simple note for the youth maker program—something I used to do without thinking—and the words and numbers just scatter on me. I try to focus, but it doesn’t stay.
Would you say that you have had days where you feel depressed most of the time, not just feeling down occasionally?

Yes. Most days I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. It’s not just being a little down. Even when my wife is being kind and talking to me, I still feel like I’m sitting at the bottom of a well.
Would you say your low mood has been present most of the day, nearly every day, since your sister passed away?

Yes. It’s been there most of the day, almost every day. I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest, and even when my wife is being kind and talking to me, I still feel like I’m down at the bottom of a well.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since your sister passed away?
Yes. Food just doesn’t seem appealing much anymore. I’ll sit with breakfast and mostly push it around, and by supper my wife is telling me I’ve hardly eaten anything all day.
Have you found that you no longer take pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like woodworking, choir planning, or fishing?

Yes. I just don’t get anything from those things now. The wood pieces are still sitting on my bench and I haven’t touched them. I’ve skipped choir planning and chess, too. Even fishing, which I used to look forward to, just feels like more effort than it’s worth. That’s not like me.
Have you noticed yourself moving or thinking more slowly than usual lately?

Yes. Everything feels slowed down. Getting out of a chair takes me a while, and when someone asks me something, I just… sit there before I can answer. It’s like my body and my words are moving through wet cement.
Before this current time, have you had any periods lasting two weeks or more where you felt similarly down, lost interest in things, or had trouble focusing?
I don’t think so. I’ve had sad stretches before, like anyone, but nothing that lasted like this or made me lose interest and concentration this much.

Other conditions like dementia (F04) or other anxiety disorders are less likely at this point given the clinical picture and duration of symptoms.

The patient's symptoms of persistent sadness, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, and difficulty concentrating since the death of their sister suggest major depressive disorder. The onset within three weeks of a significant stressor (bereavement) supports the diagnosis of a major depressive episode. The duration of symptoms (three weeks) is insufficient to diagnose recurrent depressive disorder (F33.2) at this time, but it remains a candidate if symptoms persist beyond six months. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood (F43.12) is ruled out as the symptoms extend beyond what would be expected from a normal grieving process and are significantly impairing functioning.
